goal: The user stacks tasks and has an AI work on them, the work resumes once the usage limit lifts, and the results are checked and taken in afterward. Once it's achieved, an AI stacks tasks and lets go, and afterward checks which tasks finished and which were given up, and takes their results in.

deliverable.name: The cases that check the joined parts reach the AI's aim are written

decisions.decided: A queue stacked anew waits for the next time its start hour comes; a queue stacked again to carry on its unfinished tasks starts them at once.

decisions.about: How the runner knows a queue is carried on
decisions.decided: The stacker hands the runner no start for a queue stacked again to carry on its unfinished tasks, so the runner starts them at once.

decisions.about: A task carried on and its earlier waits
decisions.decided: A task carried on keeps none of its earlier waits, as its stops at the usage limit count from zero again.

decisions.about: A queue stacked again whose every task finished
decisions.decided: Stacking again a queue whose every task finished starts no runner and says that every task finished.

decisions.about: A check while tasks still run
decisions.decided: A check while the runner still carries tasks tells each task not yet ended as still running, beside the ends of the others.

more.good_when: The developer who builds runner/schedule.py's `carry` sees a case fail where a body starts the next tasks only once all three running ones have ended, as a night whose one task waits hours at the usage limit then leaves the other tasks idle. Today every task in the three-at-a-time cases takes the same time, so such a body still passes them.

The developer sees, for any queue and any mix of how its tasks end (finished, stopped at the limit, failed, at any time), that at most three run at once, a fourth starts as soon as one ends, and every task still ends, as P4.1 and P3.2 hold for every queue. Today these hold only for the queues of one, three, and five equal tasks that the cases pick.
